title: PBX vs. VoIP: What's the difference and which is right for your business?
summary: Compare PBX vs. VoIP phone systems. Understand key differences, costs, and why most small businesses are switching to cloud VoIP.
body_markdown:
When people search "PBX vs. VoIP," they're often comparing two things that aren't quite opposites — and that confusion can lead to the wrong phone system decision. A private branch exchange (PBX) is a *system* for routing calls inside your business, while voice over internet protocol (VoIP) is the *technology* used to transmit those calls over the internet. The real choice for most businesses today is between a traditional on-premises PBX and a modern cloud VoIP system — and understanding that distinction could save you significant time, money, and headaches.

## What is a PBX phone system?


A[PBX phone system](https://www.zoom.com/en/blog/what-is-a-pbx-phone-system/) — short for private branch exchange — is the internal telephone network that lets employees share a set of external phone lines and call each other using short extensions. Before cloud technology, every business that wanted a professional phone system needed one on-site: a rack of hardware in a closet, a network of wired desk phones, and an IT team to manage it all.


Over time, PBX technology has evolved into several types:


- **Traditional (analog) PBX:** On-premises hardware wired to the public telephone network (PSTN). Reliable, but expensive to install and maintain.
- **IP PBX:** An on-premises system that uses VoIP to route calls over your internal network rather than copper phone lines — a step toward modernization, but still requires on-site hardware.
- **Cloud PBX (hosted PBX):** A PBX system that lives in the cloud and is managed by a service provider. You connect through the internet; no on-site hardware is required.


The key insight: every cloud PBX runs on VoIP. So the question isn't really "PBX or VoIP?" It's "traditional on-premises PBX or a cloud-based VoIP system?"


## What is VoIP?


Voice over internet protocol (VoIP) is the technology that converts voice into digital data packets and transmits them over the internet. Instead of routing calls over copper phone lines and the traditional PSTN network, VoIP uses your broadband connection to carry voice traffic.


[Hosted VoIP](https://www.zoom.com/en/blog/hosted-voip/) — also called a cloud phone system — takes this a step further. A third-party provider manages all the infrastructure in secure data centers, and you access your phone system through an app or a compatible desk phone. There's no server to buy, no hardware to maintain, and no IT specialist required to keep calls flowing.


Many modern business phone systems, including Zoom Phone, are hosted VoIP solutions — which means they combine the functionality of a full PBX with the simplicity of a cloud service.


## PBX vs. VoIP — it's not really either/or


PBX and VoIP are not alternatives. A PBX is a *call management system* . VoIP is a *transmission method* . Modern cloud PBX systems use VoIP to route calls; traditional PBX systems used the PSTN.


> **The real comparison:** Traditional on-premises PBX (hardware-based, PSTN-connected) vs. cloud VoIP (software-based, internet-connected).


When a small business asks "should we get a PBX or VoIP?", what they typically mean is: "Should we keep our old on-site phone hardware, or move to a cloud phone system?" That's the decision this guide helps you make.

## PBX vs. VoIP costs


Cost is often the deciding factor — and the gap between traditional on-premises and cloud VoIP is wider than many buyers expect.


According to[Zoom's business phone system cost guide](https://www.zoom.com/en/blog/how-much-does-a-business-phone-system-cost/) , traditional on-premises PBX hardware can carry an upfront investment of $5,000 to $15,000 or more, depending on the number of users and the complexity of the setup. That doesn't include installation, IT labor, ongoing maintenance, or hardware replacements when components fail.


Cloud VoIP systems, by contrast, typically run on a per-user, per-month subscription with little to no upfront hardware cost. Pricing varies by provider and feature set — check the[Zoom Phone pricing page](https://zoom.us/pricing/zoom-phone) for current plan details.


The total cost of ownership over three to five years may favor cloud VoIP for many small and mid-sized businesses — though outcomes vary based on organization size, call volume, and existing infrastructure — particularly when factoring in the elimination of hardware replacement cycles and the reduced need for on-site IT support.


## Which is better for small businesses?


For most small businesses, cloud VoIP is the stronger choice. Here's why:


**You don't need to own a server.** Traditional PBX systems require physical hardware that lives in your office. Cloud VoIP runs in the provider's data centers — your team gets a professional phone system without the infrastructure overhead.


**Your team works from anywhere.** On-premises PBX systems are built around a fixed location. Cloud VoIP works on any device with an internet connection — desktop app, mobile app, or compatible desk phone — so remote and hybrid teams stay connected without workarounds.


**Scaling is straightforward.** Adding a new employee to a traditional PBX can mean ordering hardware and waiting for installation. With cloud VoIP, adding a user is typically done through an admin portal.


**AI features are available.** Traditional PBX systems don't offer AI-powered capabilities. Modern cloud VoIP platforms can include features like call summaries, voicemail prioritization, and call questions with eligible paid plans — capabilities that help small business teams work more efficiently.


**The narrow exception:** If your business operates in an area with unreliable internet and you make very high call volumes, traditional PBX may offer more consistent call quality. For most small businesses, however, a quality internet connection makes cloud VoIP the more practical and cost-effective path.

## Frequently asked questions


### **What is the difference between PBX and VoIP?**


A PBX (private branch exchange) is a phone system that manages internal and external calls for a business. VoIP (voice over internet protocol) is the technology that transmits voice calls over the internet rather than traditional phone lines. Modern cloud PBX systems — like Zoom Phone — use VoIP as their underlying technology, so the two often go hand in hand.


### **Is VoIP better than PBX for small businesses?**


For most small businesses, cloud VoIP is the more practical choice. It eliminates expensive upfront hardware costs, works on any device from any location, scales easily as your team grows, and can include AI-powered features with eligible paid plans. Traditional on-premises PBX may suit businesses with very specific on-site reliability requirements, but it's less flexible for remote and hybrid teams.


### **What is a hosted PBX?**


A hosted PBX is a cloud-based phone system in which the PBX hardware and software are managed by a third-party provider rather than installed on your premises. You access all the features — extensions, call routing, auto attendants, voicemail — through the internet. Zoom Phone is an example of a hosted PBX solution.


### **What happens to VoIP if the internet goes down?**


If your internet connection goes down, a cloud VoIP system may be temporarily unavailable for calls made from that location. Many businesses mitigate this risk through redundant internet connections, mobile failover, or by routing calls to mobile devices. Your VoIP provider can advise on the best continuity options for your situation.


### **How does Zoom Phone compare to a traditional PBX?**


Zoom Phone operates as a full cloud PBX — it handles call routing, extensions, auto attendants, call queues, and voicemail — without requiring any on-premises hardware. Unlike traditional PBX systems, Zoom Phone works on any device, scales without hardware upgrades, and can include AI-powered call features with eligible paid plans. See[Zoom Phone's cloud PBX features](https://www.zoom.com/en/products/voip-phone/features/cloud-pbx/) for a full list of capabilities.


### **Can I keep my existing phone numbers if I switch to VoIP?**


In most cases, yes. Number porting lets you transfer your existing business phone numbers to a new VoIP provider. The process and timeline can vary depending on your current carrier and the number of lines being transferred. Your VoIP provider will typically guide you through the porting process.


## Conclusion


The PBX vs. VoIP question is really a question about where you want your phone infrastructure to live — on-site or in the cloud. For small businesses looking for flexibility, lower upfront costs, and a system that works wherever their team does, cloud VoIP is a compelling path forward.
